implementation_notes: System.Text.Json, the modern default, supports the pattern declaratively: [JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "$type")] on the base type plus one [JsonDerivedType(typeof(T), "tag")] per concrete type makes the serializer emit the discriminator and use it to select the concrete type on the way back, so the attribute set is the allow-list and no binder is involved. Before .NET 7 the same effect required a custom JsonConverter that clones the Utf8JsonReader, reads the discriminator token and calls Deserialize with the resolved type. It is still worth reading the payload with JsonDocument first when unknown tags must be quarantined rather than thrown.

variants.name: System.Text.Json attribute-declared discriminators
variants.implementation_notes: System.Text.Json, the modern default, supports the pattern declaratively: [JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "$type")] on the base type plus one [JsonDerivedType(typeof(T), "tag")] per concrete type makes the serializer emit the discriminator and use it to select the concrete type on the way back, so the attribute set is the allow-list and no binder is involved. It is still worth reading the payload with JsonDocument first when unknown tags must be quarantined rather than thrown.
variants.code_sketch:
[JsonPolymorphic(TypeDiscriminatorPropertyName = "$type")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(OrderCreated),   "order.created")]
[JsonDerivedType(typeof(OrderCancelled), "order.cancelled")]
public abstract class Event { public string Id { get; init; } = ""; }

var evt = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Event>(payload);   // $type selects the class
pitfalls: Polymorphism applies only where the declared type is the base type: serializing a concrete-typed property omits the discriminator, so a later read through the base type cannot resolve the subtype.
An unknown or missing discriminator throws JsonException instead of yielding an unknown-type value; if you need forward compatibility, read with JsonDocument/JsonNode and dispatch yourself.

variants.name: Newtonsoft.Json $type metadata with a custom binder
variants.implementation_notes: Newtonsoft.Json writes the .NET type name into the payload as a $type member (TypeNameHandling.Objects/All/Auto) and re-instantiates it on read, so the type identity is introduced by the library rather than by the message designer. Because the payload then chooses the type, the setting is a documented code-execution risk: keep TypeNameHandling.None unless the data is trusted and, when it is genuinely needed, supply an ISerializationBinder that validates every incoming type name against an allow-list - Microsoft's CA2326/CA2328 rules exist for exactly this. On .NET 7 or later prefer System.Text.Json, where the allow-list is declarative.
pitfalls: TypeNameHandling other than None without a binder lets the payload instantiate any loadable type, and gadget chains in the classpath turn that into remote code execution; the binder must deny by default.
$type values are assembly-qualified .NET names, so assembly version or strong-name changes break stored payloads even when the class itself is untouched.
